title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline to a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The confirmatory paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent clusters (75 each), declared model gpt-5-mini, and a stateless snapshot validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implementing full_intent_constraint_validation. The orchestration used a shared‑initial candidate per task (both conditions), and the guarded GVR condition could invoke ≤1 automated repair. Execution: planned 600 episodes, completed 600, model_calls_used=301 (300 shared initial calls + 1 repair); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.00333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. The preregistered target effect (absolute +0.10) was not observed; we show this null outcome follows from a near‑ceiling baseline and effectively inactive repair engagement (repair executed exactly once), and we archive all artifacts for community reuse and for designing stronger confirmatory contrasts.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are widely proposed for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, change planning, automated remediation). Prior studies demonstrate that LLMs can produce plausible configuration text but often commit syntax, topology, or semantic errors; tool‑assisted and generate–validate–repair (GVR) styles have been proposed to reduce misconfiguration risk. A reproducible, machine‑checkable benchmark that couples explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and a sealed preregistration would enable confirmatory comparisons of guarded pipelines versus single‑pass generation. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1. The final research question (preregistered) was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM? Our principal contribution is (1) the sealed task bank and deterministic validator suited for paired inference, (2) a fully archived confirmatory run (N=300 paired tasks) comparing a guarded GVR pipeline to a shared‑initial single‑pass baseline, and (3) an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining why the preregistered detectable effect was not observed.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent reviews document pronounced interest in LLMs for network management while highlighting open reliability, hallucination, and verification challenges [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical work shows LLMs can synthesize router configurations in constrained settings but typically require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Tool‑assisted generate–validate–repair approaches have demonstrated improved correction rates in focused prototypes [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], yet evaluations are dataset‑specific and limited in scale. Attack and defense studies on prompt injection and adversarial inputs motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators for operational NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our work contributes a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a preregistered paired run that ties a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a tightly specified budget and retry policy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypothesis. We froze the study as ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: GVR yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specified task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatments, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a repair budget of ≤1 automated repair per failed candidate. Task bank. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, difficulty label, and a required_sequence of atomic operations that must appear in a valid candidate. Device counts vary from 3–50; topologies and vendor models are abstracted. Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation as a stateless snapshot checker: it parses candidates into canonical field operations, enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, mutual‑exclusion, group constraints), preserves unspecified state when requested, computes the implied final_state, and emits a binary valid flag plus diagnostic traces (execution/scoring/*.json contain per‑task validator traces). Shared‑initial paired design and repair budget. To isolate repair value we used one shared initial generation per task (the identical candidate served as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline’s initial candidate). If the validator rejected that candidate the guarded pipeline could invoke up to one automated repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial design was fixed in the preregistration and intentionally prevents the guarded condition from sampling an independent alternative initial candidate. Model and invocation. The declared model is gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version/requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") invoked via the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 using provider = "openai_responses"; execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records invocation settings. Analysis plan. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed over N=300 paired binary outcomes; the preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Missingness and sensitivity treatments were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The execution manifest records: started_at_utc = 2026‑08‑29T12:41:43.384097+00:00, completed_at_utc = 2026‑08‑29T13:07:38.995000+00:00; planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) notes hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, i.e., the repair stage executed exactly once across the N=300 tasks. Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. Discordant episode and repair trace indexing. The single repair provider trace is the lone repair event recorded by the provider_call_audit. Because provider_call_audit documents 300 shared initial generation events followed by one repair event, the repair provider call corresponds to the 301st provider_call event in execution/raw_results.jsonl (authoritative provider trace container; SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Auditors can deterministically extract that 301st entry from execution/raw_results.jsonl to obtain the exact pair_id and the complete per‑call provider trace; the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json provide the cross‑references required to locate that entry. Omitted preregistered secondary estimands. The preregistration listed secondary_estimands (per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions). The archived analysis artifacts show an empty secondary_results array and no computed effect‑size artifact; accordingly these preregistered secondary estimands were not reported in the archived confirmatory analysis. The practical reason is arithmetic: the baseline margin (≈0.9967) produced an observed ceiling that made the preregistered target effect (absolute +0.10) impossible and produced only a single discordant pair (n10=1), rendering standard secondary effect‑size summaries uninformative. Statistical interpretation. The exact McNemar p depends solely on discordant pair counts (n10 and n01). With n10=1 and n01=0 the two‑sided exact p reported by the preregistered executor is 1.0; this reflects the paucity of discordant outcomes rather than a flawed test. In this ceiling regime the paired bootstrap CI (reported above) more usefully quantifies the practical uncertainty in the paired difference. Representative per‑task validator traces. Representative execution/scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001‑*.json … task-000006‑*.json) illustrate normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after traces, and validator.valid flags; the full per‑task traces and the single repair provider trace are archived in the evidence bundle for inspection.
sections.discussion: What the null result means. The confirmatory null applies to this sealed design: deterministic synthetic tasks, shared‑initial generation, snapshot deterministic validator, and a repair budget limited to one automated invocation. The guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline because the shared initial generator satisfied the validator in 299/300 cases; hence the guarded pipeline could improve only once, producing an arithmetic ceiling. This outcome does not imply GVR architectures are generically unhelpful: in settings with lower generator quality, adversarial seeds, stateful validators, or larger repair budgets, GVR is more likely to yield measurable benefit. Recommendations grounded in archived artifacts. The execution artifacts support concrete design changes to make repair efficacy measurable in future confirmatory runs: (A) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); (B) permit iterative repair budgets or multiple repair attempts per failed candidate (the provider_call_audit shows repair=1 here); (C) allow multiple independent initial generations per task to evaluate selection/reranking strategies; (D) adopt stateful/emulation validators that capture temporal side effects; (E) include explicit adversarial prompts to exercise prompt‑hardening defenses. Each recommendation maps directly to observed execution facts and to per‑task diagnostics archived in the bundle. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or selection strategies; repair rarely engaged, limiting internal contrasts. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and in‑flight temporal dynamics. External validity: tasks are synthetic and one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator version (v5.0) were evaluated; results do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the single discordant outcome leaves subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis (target +0.10) was not supported; the result follows from a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (provider_call_audit stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so future work can instantiate harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons that can demonstrate when GVR pipelines yield measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
